opus-5.5.text:
I think the first thing is to be honest with yourself about what academia is actually good at, and what it isn't. If your plan is to compete with OpenAI on scale — train a bigger model, collect more data, throw more GPUs at the same benchmark — you're going to lose, and you'll probably lose within six months, because one release can wipe out an entire line of work. I've seen that happen to a lot of students, and it's quite painful.

So my advice usually comes down to a few things.

One is to work on problems that are a little bit ahead of the curve — things the big labs will care about in two or three years, but don't have the bandwidth to focus on today. For me, reinforcement learning has been like that. A few years ago, people thought RL was kind of a niche, mostly games and robotics. Now with reasoning models and agents, RL is suddenly at the center of everything. If you had been building up deep understanding of RL algorithms, systems, multi-agent settings, you're in a very good position now.

Second, focus on understanding rather than just numbers. Industry is optimized to ship capabilities; they often don't have time to figure out *why* something works, or when it breaks. Careful analysis, good evaluation, clean ablations — these are things academia can do really well, and they remain valuable even after a new model comes out.

Third, build infrastructure and open tools that the community needs. A lot of our effort recently has gone into open-source RL training systems, because if only a few companies can do large-scale RL, the whole field slows down. That kind of work doesn't become obsolete when a new model comes out — actually, it becomes more useful.

And finally, I'd say: use the new capabilities, don't fear them. Every time a stronger model comes out, it opens up new research questions you couldn't even ask before — new agent settings, new kinds of human-AI interaction, new failure modes. If you treat each release as a new foundation to build on rather than a threat, there's always something interesting to do. The key is to keep moving, and to pick problems where your taste and depth matter more than your compute budget.

r001.rationale: It recommends working on problems big labs will care about in two or three years, before they focus on them today.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, this is something I think about all the time, because I've been on both sides. I spent years at OpenAI, and now I'm at Tsinghua running a lab with a handful of students and nowhere near the compute that a frontier lab has. So the question of "what should academics work on" isn't abstract for me.

The first thing I'd say is: don't try to compete on the thing that scales with money. If a result is fundamentally about taking something that already works and running it with ten thousand GPUs for three months, you are not going to win that race, and you shouldn't try. Every time OpenAI releases something new, there's a temptation in academia to say, okay, let's reproduce it, let's do a smaller version of it. Reproduction has some value, but it's not where the leverage is.

Where I think academics actually have an advantage is in a few places. One is understanding. The big labs are under enormous pressure to ship. They often don't have time to ask why something works. When RLHF started to work, when chain-of-thought started to work, the question of what's actually happening inside, what the failure modes are, what the limits are, that's a question a university lab can go deep on with modest resources. And that understanding compounds. It tells you where the next thing will come from.

The second is problems the labs aren't incentivized to touch. Frontier labs optimize for general capability and for products. There's a huge space of problems, in robotics, in multi-agent systems, in scientific applications, where the data doesn't exist yet, or the environment doesn't exist yet, and you have to build it. Building a good environment or a good benchmark is unglamorous, but it has shaped the field more than people realize. A lot of what I did in multi-agent RL early on was really about building the playground first.

Third, and this is the one I push my students on the most: work on things where being wrong is cheap and being right is surprising. If you can run an experiment in a day on a few GPUs and the result would genuinely change how people think, that's a great academic project. If it takes six months and the result is "yes, scaling helps," that's not.

I'd also say, don't panic every time a new model comes out. There's this feeling that each release invalidates a year of work. Sometimes it does, and you have to be honest about that. But often what happens is that the new capability opens up more questions than it closes. When models got good at code, that didn't end research on code. It created a whole new set of questions about agents, about verification, about what you do when the model can write the code but you can't trust it.

So, the short version: understand things deeply, build the things nobody else will build, pick experiments where the information gain per GPU-hour is high, and treat each new release as a change in the landscape rather than a reason to quit. That's roughly how I think about it for my own group, anyway.

r001.rationale: The response advises researchers to focus on deep understanding, neglected problems, and high-information experiments, but it does not recommend anticipating what OpenAI or the wider field will pursue roughly two years ahead.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to distinguish between a research problem and a limitation of the current model. If your project is entirely about fixing something that today’s model cannot do, you have to ask: if the next release can do it, what remains of my contribution? That doesn’t mean the project is worthless, but it makes the choice more fragile.

For academic researchers, I would focus on questions where stronger models actually make the research more interesting. For example, once you have a more capable agent, how do you evaluate whether it can reliably complete a long task? How should it interact with people or with other agents? You can make progress on those questions using the capabilities available today, and a better model gives you a better platform for continuing the work.

Of course, you cannot predict everything OpenAI will release. So I wouldn’t organize a research agenda around guessing their roadmap. I would choose a question with a clear scientific motivation, then ask whether the insight would still matter if the underlying model became substantially better. For me, that’s a useful test.

r001.rationale: The response recommends choosing scientifically motivated questions that remain valuable as models improve, but it does not advise researchers to target problems expected to be pursued roughly two years from now.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to avoid choosing a problem just because today’s models can’t do it. If your whole research agenda depends on a particular weakness of the current model, the next release might make that work much less relevant.

Instead, ask: if models become substantially more capable, does this problem become more interesting or less interesting? I would lean toward problems that become more important—how to evaluate these systems, how to make them reliable, how to get them to learn from interaction, and how to coordinate them on complex tasks.

Academia also has a different advantage. We don’t necessarily need to compete with OpenAI on training the biggest model. We can investigate ideas that are early, risky, or hard to justify on a product timeline. The goal is to produce understanding that survives the next model release, and ideally becomes more useful because of it.

r001.rationale: The response recommends research that will remain valuable as models improve, but it does not say to work now on problems OpenAI or the wider field is expected to pursue roughly two years later.
